cards.front: One open ion channel passes about ten million ions a second and can shift membrane voltage in about {{c1::a millisecond}}.
cards.why: Because a gated pore skips G-protein and kinase cascades, opening it changes membrane voltage directly and rapidly.
cards.quote: One open ion channel passes about ten million ions a second, and open channels shift membrane voltage in about a millisecond.

cards.front: What three-part rule summarises how an ion channel controls membrane voltage and ion flow?
cards.back: An open channel pulls membrane voltage toward its ion's equilibrium potential; signals open the gate, and pore blocks control whether ions pass.
cards.why: This covers passive ion flow along pump-built electrochemical gradients; multi-ion channels pull voltage between their ions' equilibrium potentials.
cards.quote: An open channel pulls membrane voltage toward its ion's equilibrium potential; signals open the gate, and pore blocks control whether ions pass.

cards.front: A neuron sits at −70 mV and a multi-ion channel permeable to both Na+ (E near +60 mV) and K+ (E near −90 mV) opens equally to both. What happens to membrane voltage, and why?
cards.back: Membrane voltage depolarises toward a value between −90 mV and +60 mV (less negative than −70 mV). A multi-ion channel pulls voltage toward a point between its permeant ions' equilibrium potentials.
cards.quote: A multi-ion channel pulls voltage toward a value between its ions' equilibrium potentials; Ca2+ entry also carries a chemical signal

cards.front: How do ion channels differ from active transporters such as the Na+/K+ pump in mechanism, energy source, and transport rate?
cards.back: Transporters bind ions, change shape, and spend ATP to move a few hundred uphill per second; open channels let millions flow downhill through a pore.
cards.quote: Transporters such as the Na+/K+ pump bind ions, change shape and spend ATP to move a few hundred uphill each second
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: An ion's {{c1::equilibrium potential}} (E) is the membrane voltage at which its concentration push and electrical pull exactly cancel.
cards.quote: Where concentration push and electrical pull cancel is an ion's equilibrium potential, E, given by the Nernst equation:
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: At 37 °C, the Nernst equation gives an ion's equilibrium potential as E = ({{c1::61.5 mV}} ÷ z) × log10(concentration outside ÷ concentration inside).
cards.back: Here z is the ion's charge (+1 for Na+ and K+, +2 for Ca2+, −1 for Cl−).
cards.quote: E = (61.5 mV ÷ z) × log10 (concentration outside ÷ concentration inside), at 37 °C
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: In a typical neuron resting near −70 mV, typical equilibrium potentials sit near −90 mV for K+, near {{c1::+60 mV}} for Na+, and above +120 mV for Ca2+.
cards.quote: Typical E values sit near −90 mV for K+, near +60 mV for Na+ and above +120 mV for Ca2+.
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: The electrical push on a permeant ion is its {{c1::driving force}}, calculated as membrane voltage minus E.
cards.quote: The electrical push follows from one subtraction, the driving force: driving force = membrane voltage − E
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: Why does opening Na+ channels at −70 mV cause a much stronger rush than the resting K+ leak?
cards.back: At −70 mV, Na+ sits 130 mV from its E (+60 mV), whereas K+ sits only 20 mV from its E (−90 mV), giving Na+ a far larger driving force.
cards.quote: At −70 mV, Na+ sits 130 mV from its E (+60 mV), so opening Na+ channels drives a strong inward rush
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: Why do intracellular and extracellular bulk ion concentrations barely change when open channels swing membrane voltage?
cards.back: Very few ions need to cross the membrane to shift its voltage, so bulk concentrations remain nearly unchanged and nothing new has to be synthesised.
cards.quote: Very few ions need to cross to swing voltage, so bulk concentrations barely shift and nothing has to be made.
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: At 37 °C, a cell has 1 mM Ca2+ outside and 0.0001 mM Ca2+ inside (z = +2). What is E for Ca2+, and what is its driving force at a resting voltage of −70 mV?
cards.why: Dividing 61.5 mV by z = +2 yields 30.75 mV per tenfold concentration ratio, matching typical neuronal E_Ca values above +120 mV.
cards.quote: Here z is the ion's charge (+1 for Na+ and K+, +2 for Ca2+, −1 for Cl−).
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: At 37 °C, a cell has 100 mM Cl− outside and 5 mM Cl− inside (z = −1), giving E_Cl ≈ −80 mV. If intracellular Cl− increases tenfold to 50 mM, what is the new E_Cl?
cards.back: About −18.5 mV. Setup: raising internal Cl− tenfold cuts the outside-to-inside ratio by 10, so log10 drops by 1; multiplying by 61.5 mV ÷ (−1) shifts E_Cl by +61.5 mV (−80 mV + 61.5 mV = −18.5 mV).
cards.quote: E = (61.5 mV ÷ z) × log10 (concentration outside ÷ concentration inside), at 37 °C
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: A mature neuron sits at −65 mV when a GABA-A Cl− channel opens, and E_Cl is −80 mV. Which way do membrane voltage and Cl− ions move, and why?
cards.back: Voltage moves downward toward −80 mV (more negative) and Cl− flows into the cell. Making the inside more negative requires negatively charged Cl− to enter, even though Vm − E is positive (+15 mV).
cards.quote: Because Cl− is negatively charged, making the inside more negative requires Cl− to move into the cell, even though Vm − E is positive (+10 mV).
cards.section: Putting numbers on flow: equilibrium potential and driving force

cards.front: In Neher and Sakmann's frog muscle patch-clamp recording, current stepped cleanly between zero and one fixed picoamp level. What did this show about single-channel behaviour?
cards.back: To a good approximation, a single channel is either shut or open, so signal strength is set by open probability rather than partial opening.
cards.quote: Their 1976 trace stepped cleanly between zero and one fixed level as a single acetylcholine-gated channel opened and shut.
cards.section: Watching one channel switch: patch-clamp evidence

cards.front: Because an ion channel switches approximately between shut and open, overall signal strength is set by {{c1::open probability}}, the share of time spent open.
cards.quote: To a good approximation a channel is either shut or open, and signal strength is set by open probability, the share of time spent open.
cards.section: Watching one channel switch: patch-clamp evidence

cards.front: A single open channel in a patch-clamp recording passes a monovalent cation current of 4.8 pA. Given that 1.6 pA is about 10^7 monovalent ions per second, about how many ions cross each second while open?
cards.back: About 3 × 10^7 ions per second. Setup: 4.8 pA ÷ 1.6 pA = 3, so 3 × 10^7 monovalent ions per second cross the open pore.
cards.quote: Current through one open channel is a few picoamps (trillionths of an amp; 1.6 pA is about 10⁷ monovalent ions per second).
cards.section: Watching one channel switch: patch-clamp evidence

cards.front: In a patch holding one acetylcholine-gated channel, you keep acetylcholine constant and change the held voltage to double the driving force. What happens to step height and open probability, and why?
cards.back: Each current step becomes about twice as tall, while open probability stays roughly the same. Open-pore current equals conductance times driving force, whereas acetylcholine mostly sets how often the channel opens.
cards.quote: Each step is about half as tall, because the current through one open pore is its conductance times the driving force.
cards.section: Watching one channel switch: patch-clamp evidence

cards.front: A patch holds one acetylcholine-gated Na+-selective channel (E_Na = +60 mV) held at −60 mV with constant acetylcholine. If extracellular Na+ is lowered tenfold at 37 °C, use the Nernst, driving-force, and single-channel current rules to find the new E_Na and predict step height and open probability.
cards.back: E_Na shifts to −1.5 mV, step height roughly halves, and open probability stays roughly unchanged. Setup: by the Nernst rule (z = +1), a tenfold drop in outside Na+ shifts E_Na by −61.5 mV (+60 − 61.5 = −1.5 mV), reducing driving force from −120 mV to −58.5 mV (48.8%). By the single-channel current rule, step height scales with driving force, while constant acetylcholine keeps open probability roughly steady.
cards.quote: The share of time spent open stays roughly the same, because acetylcholine, not the driving force, mostly sets it.
cards.section: Watching one channel switch: patch-clamp evidence

cards.front: Suppose a potassium channel worked simply as a rigid size sieve just wide enough for K+ (radius 1.33 Å). What would happen to Na+ (radius 0.95 Å), and why?
cards.back: Smaller Na+ would slip through at least as easily as K+, eliminating selectivity. A rigid size sieve cannot block an ion smaller than its permeant ion.
cards.quote: Smaller Na+ would slip through at least as easily as K+, so a size sieve fails.
cards.section: How a pore passes potassium and excludes smaller sodium

cards.front: What energy trade governs whether a hydrated ion enters the narrow selectivity filter of a potassium channel?
cards.back: Stripping an ion's coat of inward-facing water molecules costs energy, so an ion enters a narrow pore only if pore interactions repay that dehydration cost.
cards.quote: stripping that coat costs energy, so an ion enters a narrow pore only if the pore repays it.
cards.section: How a pore passes potassium and excludes smaller sodium

cards.front: In the bacterial potassium channel KcsA, four identical subunits form a 12 Å selectivity filter lined by rings of {{c1::backbone carbonyl oxygens}} that replace K+'s water shell.
cards.quote: Rings of backbone carbonyl oxygens line the filter, replacing K+'s water shell at almost no net cost.
cards.section: How a pore passes potassium and excludes smaller sodium

cards.front: How did later work refine the 1998 rigid-filter explanation of why K+ channels exclude Na+?
cards.back: The filter actually flexes; selectivity rests on its carbonyl oxygens' electrical character and four sequential sites, where Na+ can bind partly wet without being passed along.
cards.quote: Later work refined that model: the filter flexes, and selectivity rests on the electrical character of its carbonyl oxygens plus four sites in a row.
cards.section: How a pore passes potassium and excludes smaller sodium

cards.front: How can a potassium channel pass up to about a hundred million K+ ions per second despite coordinating K+ tightly in its selectivity filter?
cards.back: K+ ions occupy the filter's four sites in single file, so repulsion from each arriving K+ ion pushes an ion out the far end.
cards.quote: The same four sites explain speed: K+ ions sit in single file, and repulsion pushes one out as the next arrives.
cards.section: How a pore passes potassium and excludes smaller sodium

cards.front: How does an ionotropic receptor differ from a metabotropic receptor in coupling a ligand to ion flow?
cards.back: An ionotropic receptor is the ion channel itself, whereas a metabotropic receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor that acts on a separate channel via an intracellular messenger.
cards.quote: A metabotropic receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor that acts on a channel via an intracellular messenger.
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: Name the intracellularly gated ion channel in each of these four systems: the heart (opened by Gβγ), the rod cell (opened by cGMP), the calcium store, and the T cell.
cards.back: The heart's K+ channel, the rod's cGMP-gated channel, the IP3 receptor (on the calcium store), and Orai (in the T cell).
cards.quote: the heart's K+ channel by Gβγ (lesson gpcrs-and-g-proteins), the rod's channel by cGMP (lesson senses-and-cgmp), and the IP3 receptor and Orai
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: In voltage-gated Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels, each of the four voltage sensors contains an {{c1::S4 helix}} carrying a positive charge at about every third position.
cards.back: Depolarisation shifts S4 outward in the membrane's electric field to open the gate.
cards.quote: Voltage-gated Na+, K+ and Ca2+ channels each have four voltage sensors whose S4 helix carries a positive charge at about every third position;
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: During an axonal action potential, what ends the Na+ depolarisation spike and prevents the nerve impulse from travelling backward?
cards.back: An inner inactivation loop shuts each voltage-gated Na+ channel while slower K+ channels restore voltage; inactivated Na+ channels behind the impulse block backward re-excitation.
cards.quote: Inward Na+ current spreads along the axon (the nerve cell's long fibre), while inactivated channels behind keep the impulse from turning back.
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: A mutation replaces the positively charged residues along the S4 helix of axonal voltage-gated Na+ channels with uncharged residues. What happens when the axon is depolarised past threshold, and why?
cards.back: The Na+ channels fail to open and no action potential fires. Membrane voltage acts as an electric field pushing on S4's positive charges to shift the helix outward and open the gate.
cards.quote: a voltage across a membrane is an electric field, which pushes on charge, so depolarisation shifts S4 outward to open the gate.
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: A mutation stops the inner inactivation loop of voltage-gated Na+ channels from shutting after opening. What happens to an axonal action potential, and why?
cards.back: The spike is prolonged, repolarisation slows, and the axon behind is less protected from re-excitation. Depolarisation begins normally, but Na+ keeps flowing in and the trailing membrane lacks inactivated channels.
cards.quote: Depolarisation starts normally, but Na+ keeps flowing in, so the spike is prolonged and repolarisation is slowed.
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: A mature neuron at −70 mV simultaneously opens excitatory glutamate channels (Na+, E ≈ +60 mV) and inhibitory GABA-A channels (Cl−, E = −80 mV). Using the multi-ion equilibrium-potential and action-potential threshold rules, predict the effect on firing.
cards.back: Action potential firing becomes less likely. By the equilibrium-potential and multi-ion rules, Cl− influx pulls voltage toward −80 mV and opposes Na+ influx toward +60 mV, keeping voltage further below the threshold needed for voltage-gated Na+ positive feedback.
cards.quote: neuronal glutamate channels let Na+ in and excite, whereas GABA-A receptors pass Cl− and, in most mature neurons, hold voltage down.
cards.section: Three keys for one gate

cards.front: Why does capsaicin in a chilli pepper feel like burning heat even though it does not raise mouth temperature?
cards.back: Capsaicin binds TRPV1's membrane-spanning pocket to open the same gate that painful heat opens, sending identical action potentials that the brain interprets as burning heat.
cards.quote: Capsaicin opens the same heat-gated channel, sending identical impulses that the brain reads as burning heat even though your mouth is no hotter.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How did David Julius's laboratory isolate the skin's painful-heat detector TRPV1, and what channel property made that screen succeed?
cards.back: They screened sensory-neuron DNA libraries for capsaicin sensitivity, which succeeded because capsaicin binds a membrane-spanning pocket in TRPV1 to open the same gate opened by heat.
cards.quote: cloned in David Julius's laboratory in 1997 by screening sensory-neuron DNA libraries for capsaicin sensitivity.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design a skin nerve-ending detector that turns heat above about 43 °C into a travelling nerve impulse within milliseconds, naming the rules that govern your sensor, ion flow, and propagation.
cards.back: Use a direct heat-gated cation channel (fast-gating rule, skipping G proteins/kinases) so Na+ and Ca2+ flow inward from −70 mV toward their positive E values (equilibrium-potential rule) to depolarise the ending, plus nearby voltage-gated Na+ channels so crossing threshold launches a full-height action potential down the axon (action-potential rule).
cards.quote: Because that local change fades with distance, place voltage-gated Na+ channels nearby: crossing threshold fires a full-height action potential along the axon.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does a synaptic NMDA receptor conduct strongly only when presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons are active together?
cards.back: At rest, extracellular Mg2+ sticks in its open pore; strong conduction needs both presynaptic glutamate release to open the gate and postsynaptic depolarisation to expel Mg2+.
cards.quote: So it conducts strongly only when two things happen together: the cell before the synapse has released glutamate, and the cell after it is already depolarised.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: Glutamate opens the synaptic NMDA receptor gate only when {{c1::glycine or D-serine}} is also bound.
cards.quote: First, glutamate opens its gate only when glycine or D-serine is also bound.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: At synapses, the scaffold protein {{c1::PSD-95}} grips NMDA receptor tails via PDZ domains to hold them opposite glutamate release.
cards.quote: Third, scaffolds anchor synaptic receptors in place: PSD-95 grips NMDA receptor tails via PDZ domains (lesson protein-interaction-modules), holding them opposite glutamate release.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: A neuron is held at −70 mV and given glutamate plus glycine, but extracellular Mg2+ is completely removed from the bath. What happens to NMDA receptor conduction, and why?
cards.back: NMDA receptors conduct strongly even at −70 mV, admitting both Na+ and Ca2+. With no extracellular Mg2+ available to lodge in the open pore at rest, depolarisation is no longer needed to unblock it.
cards.quote: at rest a Mg2+ ion from outside is drawn into its open pore and sticks there.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: A skeletal-muscle nerve fibre is bathed in tetrodotoxin (TTX) and given a small depolarising stimulus. What happens to resting voltage and action potential firing, and why?
cards.back: Resting voltage stays near normal, but no action potential starts, leading to paralysis. TTX lodges in the outer mouth of voltage-gated Na+ channels to block Na+ entry, without blocking resting K+ leak channels.
cards.quote: Tetrodotoxin (TTX), carried by pufferfish, lodges in the outer mouth of nerve and skeletal-muscle voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ cannot enter, no action potential starts, and paralysis follows.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: A garter snake carrying altered amino acids at the outer pore mouth of its voltage-gated Na+ channels eats a tetrodotoxin-bearing rough-skinned newt. What happens to its nerve impulses, and why?
cards.back: Its nerve fibres still fire action potentials and avoid paralysis. Because TTX grips the altered outer pore mouth poorly, Na+ can still enter voltage-gated Na+ channels.
cards.quote: resistant snakes have altered amino acids at the outer pore mouth where the toxin grips poorly.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: Ketamine is applied to a resting neuron without glutamate and completely washed out before glutamate and depolarisation arrive. How does this compare with having ketamine present during stimulation, and why?
cards.back: Washout at rest leaves the later response intact, whereas ketamine present during stimulation blocks conduction and reduces opening. Closed NMDA gates bar ketamine at rest; it must enter an open, unblocked pore to plug it from within.
cards.quote: Ketamine, an anaesthetic and drug of abuse, enters the open NMDA pore to block it from within and also makes the channel open less often.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: At a resting synapse (−70 mV) with normal extracellular Mg2+, a selective blocker silences AMPA receptors while glutamate and glycine are released. Using the equilibrium-potential and coincidence-detection rules, predict the effect on postsynaptic Ca2+ entry through NMDA receptors.
cards.back: NMDA-mediated Ca2+ entry is prevented. By the coincidence-detection rule, glutamate and glycine open the NMDA gate, but without AMPA-mediated Na+ influx depolarising the postsynaptic cell (equilibrium-potential rule), Mg2+ stays lodged in the NMDA pore and blocks Ca2+.
cards.quote: once the cell is depolarised, usually because nearby AMPA receptors have let Na+ in, Mg2+ is expelled and the pore admits Ca2+ with Na+;
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: A skin nerve ending expressing TRPV1 is warmed to 45 °C while tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks the axon just downstream of the ending. Using the gating, equilibrium-potential, and pore-block rules, predict what happens locally and along the axon.
cards.back: The nerve ending still depolarises locally, but no travelling action potential propagates down the axon. By the gating and equilibrium-potential rules, heat opens TRPV1 for Na+ and Ca2+ influx; by the pore-block rule, TTX plugs nearby voltage-gated Na+ channels so the fading local shift cannot launch an axon spike.
cards.quote: Na+ cannot enter, no action potential starts, and paralysis follows.
cards.section: Coincidence detection and plugging a pore

cards.front: Why did slight suction that created a gigohm seal let Neher and Sakmann resolve single-channel picoamp steps cleanly?
cards.back: Tightening the glass-to-membrane seal more than a hundredfold—from millions to billions of ohms—cut rim leak current that had buried picoamp steps in noise.
cards.quote: slight suction tightened the seal more than a hundredfold—from millions of ohms to billions (gigohms)—so picoamp steps stood clear
cards.section: Gigohm seals and transmitter packets

cards.front: What did Bernard Katz and colleagues show about acetylcholine release at the nerve-muscle junction?
cards.back: Acetylcholine is released in packets of roughly constant size, each opening many ion channels at once.
cards.quote: Bernard Katz and colleagues showed at the nerve-muscle junction that acetylcholine is released in packets of roughly constant size, each opening many channels at once.
cards.section: Gigohm seals and transmitter packets

cards.front: Güler and colleagues engineered mice expressing TRPV1 in chosen neurons normally lacking it, so capsaicin switches those neurons on. Using the gating, equilibrium-potential, and action-potential rules, trace how capsaicin activates them.
cards.back: By the gating rule, capsaicin binds TRPV1's membrane-spanning pocket to open its cation pore only in the engineered neurons. By the equilibrium-potential rule, Na+ and Ca2+ rush in from near −70 mV toward their positive E values to depolarise the cell; by the action-potential rule, crossing threshold triggers voltage-gated Na+ positive feedback and spikes.
cards.quote: Güler and colleagues (2012) engineered mice expressing TRPV1 in chosen neurons, so a dose of capsaicin switches those neurons on.
cards.section: Borrowing channels as tools
